triage.name: Hordeolum
triage.reason: Focal painful eyelid swelling diagnosed by inspection and history; good dermatology/primary care case with chalazion as the main look-alike.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Pain on blinking' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Eyelid tenderness' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Extraocular movements normal' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Common in children and young adults
More frequent in contact lens wearers
exposures: Touching or rubbing the eyelids with unclean hands

chief_complaints.text: My eyelid is swollen and sore
There is a tender bump on my eyelid
My eye is red and watery

hpi.progression: Starts as a localized tender area on the eyelid margin, then becomes a red, swollen bump that may point and drain
hpi.location: Eyelid margin, either upper or lower eyelid
hpi.quality: Tender, warm, swollen bump; may feel like a small pimple

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not localize the pain and present with eyelid swelling, irritability, and refusal to open the eye.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of a tender bump

atypical.how_it_differs: May have less pain and more chronic eyelid margin inflammation; consider chalazion or malignancy if persistent.
Can progress rapidly to preseptal or orbital cellulitis with fever and systemic symptoms.

general.mild: Comfortable, no systemic symptoms, eyelid slightly swollen
general.moderate: Mild discomfort, keeps eye partially closed, no systemic symptoms
general.severe: Ill-appearing with marked eyelid swelling, may have fever or systemic symptoms
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with fever, proptosis, or inability to open the eye

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelids with the patient looking straight ahead
findings.finding: Localized swelling of the eyelid margin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelid skin and margin
findings.finding: Erythema of the skin of the eyelid

findings.maneuver: Palpate the eyelid margin with a finger
findings.finding: A small, firm, tender nodule at the eyelid margin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelid margin with a light and magnification
findings.finding: A small pustule or yellow-white head at the eyelid margin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva
Observe the eye for excessive tearing
Check visual acuity with a Snellen chart
Shine a light into each eye and observe the pupillary response
findings.finding: Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to follow your finger in all directions of gaze
findings.finding: Extraocular movements are full and painless

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyes from above and below for forward displacement of the globe
Palpate the preauricular, submandibular, and cervical lymph nodes

not_indicated.why: No systemic symptoms; a white count does not change management of a simple hordeolum
Inflammatory markers are not needed for a focal eyelid infection
Not useful in a self-limited eyelid infection
Routine culture of a draining stye does not change management
Not needed unless orbital or preseptal cellulitis is suspected
Reserved for suspected orbital extension or an atypical mass
Not required for a typical eyelid margin lesion

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory or imaging test is required for a typical hordeolum
Check visual acuity, pupils, and extraocular movements to separate a simple hordeolum from preseptal or orbital cellulitis
Consider imaging and systemic antibiotics if there is fever, proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, or vision loss
Refer or biopsy a persistent eyelid margin lesion that does not resolve, to exclude chalazion or malignancy

differential.name: Chalazion
differential.why_considered: Both cause a focal eyelid lump; chalazion is the most common look-alike and is often confused with an internal hordeolum.

history: Gradual, painless swelling over weeks rather than days
No acute tenderness or redness at onset
May have had a prior stye that resolved
exam: Firm, non-tender nodule within the eyelid away from the margin
Overlying skin is normal or only mildly erythematous

differential.name: Preseptal cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Eyelid swelling and redness can mimic a hordeolum, but preseptal cellulitis is a spreading infection that needs systemic antibiotics.
differential.trigger: Diffuse, not focal, eyelid swelling with fever or a recent skin break or sinus infection

history: Rapidly progressive swelling over hours to a day
Fever, malaise, or recent upper respiratory infection or eyelid trauma
Pain is diffuse rather than a single tender point
exam: Diffuse erythema and edema of the entire eyelid, not a discrete margin nodule
No proptosis, normal extraocular movements, and normal visual acuity
labs: CBC may show leukocytosis if systemic symptoms are present
imaging: CT orbits with contrast if orbital extension is suspected

differential.name: Orbital cellulitis
differential.why_considered: A severe eyelid infection can extend behind the orbital septum; this is the most dangerous look-alike and must be excluded.
differential.trigger: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, vision loss, or a toxic-appearing patient

history: Rapidly worsening eye pain and swelling
Recent sinusitis, dental infection, or eyelid trauma
exam: Decreased visual acuity or an afferent pupillary defect
imaging: CT orbits with contrast showing orbital fat stranding, abscess, or sinusitis
MRI orbits with contrast if intracranial extension is suspected

differential.name: Blepharitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic eyelid margin inflammation can cause redness, crusting, and irritation that may be mistaken for a recurrent stye.

history: Chronic, bilateral, burning or itchy eyelid margins
Crusting or flaking along the lashes, worse in the morning
Recurrent episodes rather than a single acute tender bump
exam: Diffuse eyelid margin erythema and scaling or collarettes around the lashes
No discrete tender nodule or pustule

differential.name: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
differential.why_considered: Can cause painful eyelid swelling and redness, but the vesicular rash and dermatomal distribution distinguish it.

history: Burning or tingling pain preceding a rash
Vesicular rash in the V1 dermatome
exam: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base respecting the midline
Hutchinson sign (vesicles on the nose tip) suggests ocular involvement
May have corneal involvement on slit lamp
labs: PCR of vesicle fluid for varicella-zoster virus if diagnosis is unclear

differential.name: Eyelid malignancy (e.g., basal cell carcinoma)
differential.why_considered: A persistent eyelid lesion that does not resolve can be a malignancy rather than a stye.
differential.trigger: An eyelid lesion that persists beyond 4–6 weeks, ulcerates, or bleeds

exam: Pearl-like nodule with telangiectasias, central ulceration, or loss of lashes

severity.mild: Small, localized tender eyelid margin bump with minimal redness and no visual symptoms; resolves with warm compresses.
severity.moderate: Larger, more painful swelling with erythema and tearing; may have a visible pustule but no systemic symptoms.
severity.severe: Marked eyelid swelling with fever, diffuse erythema, or inability to open the eye; consider preseptal or orbital cellulitis.
severity.critical: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, vision loss, or toxic appearance suggesting orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests orbital cellulitis or another orbital process; needs urgent imaging and antibiotics.
Orbital involvement; requires urgent ophthalmology evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Decreased visual acuity or afferent pupillary defect
red_flags.meaning: Optic nerve or orbital involvement; sight-threatening emergency.
Preseptal or orbital cellulitis rather than a simple hordeolum.

red_flags.finding: Lesion persisting beyond 4–6 weeks or ulcerating
red_flags.meaning: Consider chalazion or malignancy; biopsy or refer.

complications.name: Chalazion formation
clues: Persistent firm, non-tender eyelid nodule after acute inflammation resolves

special_populations.differences: Young children may not localize pain and present with eyelid swelling, irritability, and refusal to open the eye; monitor for rapid progression to cellulitis.
May have less pain and more chronic eyelid margin inflammation; persistent lesions should raise concern for chalazion or malignancy.
Higher risk of rapid progression to preseptal or orbital cellulitis; lower threshold for systemic antibiotics and imaging.
Increased risk of recurrent styes and more severe infections; optimize glycemic control and monitor closely.

key_questions.question: When did the eyelid swelling start, and how quickly has it changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over 1–2 days; rapid progression over hours suggests preseptal or orbital cellulitis

key_questions.question: Is the swelling a single tender spot or the whole eyelid?
key_questions.looking_for: A focal, tender bump at the eyelid margin rather than diffuse swelling

key_questions.question: Does it hurt, and does it hurt when you blink?
key_questions.looking_for: Tenderness and pain with blinking; painless nodule suggests chalazion

key_questions.question: Is your vision normal, or is it blurry or lost?
key_questions.looking_for: Normal or only mildly blurry vision; vision loss is a red flag for orbital involvement

key_questions.question: Do you have a fever, chills, or feel generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in a simple hordeolum; fever suggests preseptal or orbital cellulitis

key_questions.question: Does your eye bulge out, or is it painful or hard to move your eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; proptosis or painful or limited eye movements suggests orbital cellulitis

key_questions.question: Have you had a stye or chalazion before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior episodes suggest recurrent hordeola, blepharitis, or rosacea

key_questions.question: Do you wear contact lenses, and do you sleep or swim in them?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens wear is a risk factor and raises concern for a corneal process

key_questions.question: Do you use eye makeup, and do you remove it before bed?
key_questions.looking_for: Eye makeup use and poor eyelid hygiene are risk factors

key_questions.question: Do you have rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, or diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: Associated conditions that predispose to eyelid margin inflammation and recurrent styes

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent eye surgery, trauma, or sinus infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present raises concern for preseptal or orbital cellulitis

key_questions.question: Any discharge from the eye, or does it feel like something is in it?
key_questions.looking_for: Tearing and foreign body sensation are common; purulent discharge suggests another cause

reasoning_points: A focal, tender, red swelling at the eyelid margin that developed over 1–2 days
Pain with blinking and tenderness over the eyelid margin
Possible small pustule or yellow-white head at the eyelid margin
Vision, pupils, and extraocular movements are normal
No fever, proptosis, or systemic symptoms
Distinguished from chalazion (painless, firm, chronic nodule) and from preseptal or orbital cellulitis (diffuse swelling, fever, proptosis, vision changes)

easy: Young adult or child with a classic tender red bump at the eyelid margin
Onset over 1–2 days with pain on blinking
Normal vision and no systemic symptoms
Visible pustule at the eyelid margin
medium: Internal hordeolum with a tender nodule on the conjunctival side of the eyelid
Recurrent styes with underlying blepharitis or rosacea
Contact lens wearer with tearing and foreign body sensation
Mild conjunctival injection and blurred vision that resolves with blinking
hard: Young child who cannot localize pain and presents with eyelid swelling and irritability
Older adult with a less painful, more chronic eyelid margin lesion that could be a chalazion or malignancy
Patient with diabetes or immunocompromise and rapidly worsening swelling concerning for cellulitis
Lesion that persists beyond 4–6 weeks and needs referral or biopsy
